title: What CPD does Ahpra require, and how should employers evidence it?
description: What the National Boards' CPD registration standards require of registered health practitioners, the 2026 review, and what employers should record.
shortAnswer: Under section 128 of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, every registered health practitioner in Australia must complete the continuing professional development (CPD) set by their National Board's registration standard. Requirements differ by board: nurses and midwives need at least 20 hours a year and doctors 50 hours a year. Practitioners declare compliance at each renewal and may be audited. Employers do not own the obligation, but they verify registration and supply much of the learning.
keyTakeaways: CPD is a personal obligation of each practitioner under section 128 of the National Law. Failing to do it is not an offense but may lead to health, conduct or performance action, and a Board may refuse renewal under section 112.

Each of the 15 National Boards sets its own CPD registration standard, administered with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra). The Nursing and Midwifery Board requires 20 hours a year, the Medical Board 50 hours a year through an accredited CPD home, and the Pharmacy Board 40 credits a year.
The Nursing and Midwifery Board says routine annual CPR and mandatory fire training cannot be counted as CPD, so an employer's mandatory training calendar is not a CPD program.

Ahpra and 14 National Boards consulted from May 15 to July 17, 2026 on a common draft standard of 20 hours a year with 5 interactive hours. As at November 2026 it has not been approved, and the Medical Board is not part of the review.

Employers should verify registration on the public register, record in-service education in a form practitioners can use as CPD evidence, and keep their own training records separate from practitioners' CPD portfolios.
regulator: Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) and the 15 National Boards
appliesTo: Registered health practitioners in every profession regulated under the National Registration and Accreditation Scheme, except students and practitioners with non-practising registration
Hospitals, aged care providers, general practices, pharmacies and other employers of registered practitioners, as the main providers of workplace learning and the parties that verify registration
Education, quality and credentialing teams that report on workforce competence

sections.heading: What is the legal basis for CPD in Australian health regulation?

blocks.text: The legal basis is the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, as in force in each state and territory. Section 128(1) says "A registered health practitioner must undertake the continuing professional development required by an approved registration standard for the health profession in which the practitioner is registered." Section 128(2) adds that a contravention "does not constitute an offence but may constitute behaviour for which health, conduct or performance action may be taken", and section 128(3) excludes practitioners with non-practising registration ([National Law, Queensland reprint](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-2009-045)).

The National Law also ties CPD to renewal. Under section 109(1)(a)(iii), every renewal application must include a declaration that the applicant has completed the CPD required by the registration standard during the preceding period of registration. Under section 112(2)(c), a National Board may refuse to renew registration if the practitioner failed to complete that CPD, and under section 112(2)(d) if the annual statement was false or misleading in a material particular.

The content of each obligation sits in a profession specific registration standard approved by health ministers, supported by board guidelines. Ahpra's [CPD registration standards page](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/Registration/Registration-Standards/CPD.aspx) links to each board's standard and describes the shared purpose: practitioners "are required to participate regularly in CPD that is relevant to their scope of practice".

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the National Law, board standards and Ahpra consultation material as at November 2026. The common CPD standard proposed in 2026 had not been approved at that date. Check the board's own site before relying on a figure.

sections.heading: How many CPD hours does each National Board require?

blocks.text: The most common requirement is 20 hours a year, but the figure ranges from 20 hours a year to 50 hours a year, and two boards use a three year cycle. Ahpra's 2026 consultation paper summarizes the current position: eight National Boards require 20 hours a year, the Dental Board and the Medical Radiation Practice Board require 60 hours over three years, the Osteopathy Board requires 25 hours a year, and the Paramedicine and Psychology Boards require 30 hours a year. The Pharmacy Board is the only board that counts credits rather than hours.

Interns and doctors in a formal accredited PGY2 program are deemed to meet the Medical Board standard through their training.

sections.heading: Does workplace mandatory training count as CPD?

blocks.text: Usually not for nurses and midwives, and only when it involves new learning. The NMBA fact sheet says mandatory workplace learning can be counted "provided that they are relevant to your context of practice and where they include new learning", and gives the example that "routine annual CPR and mandatory fire training education cannot be counted". It contrasts this with genuinely new content, such as early COVID-19 pandemic education, which could be claimed.

Other boards draw the line differently. The Pharmacy Board's FAQ allows a first aid refresher to be claimed and accepts in-house workplace education where it meets the pharmacist's CPD plan. The Medical Board requires most hours to come from reviewing performance and measuring outcomes, so attendance at hospital education sessions can fill only part of a doctor's 50 hours. An employer that serves several professions therefore cannot apply one rule to every course in its catalog.

The practical consequence is that an organization's [mandatory training](/glossary/mandatory-training) program and practitioners' CPD are related but separate. Mandatory training meets the employer's own duties, such as those under the [NSQHS Standards](/regulations/nsqhs-standards-workforce-training) or work health and safety law. CPD meets the practitioner's registration duty. Some activities serve both; many do not.

sections.heading: What is the employer's role if CPD is the practitioner's obligation?

blocks.text: The employer's role is to confirm that each practitioner is registered and unrestricted for the role, to provide learning that practitioners can use, and to keep its own records of what it delivered. No registration standard makes an employer responsible for an employee's CPD hours, and Ahpra audits the practitioner, not the employer.

items: **Verify registration and conditions.** The NMBA's [renewal fact sheet for employers](https://www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au/Registration-and-Endorsement/Registration-Renewal/Renewal-FAQ-for-employers) says a listing on the national register is proof of registration and points employers to the Practitioner Information Exchange (PIE) service for bulk checks. Conditions on the register can include completing specified further education or training within a specified period.

**Know the renewal calendar.** Nurses and midwives renew by May 31 each year and remain registered for one month after expiry if they apply in that late period; after that, registration lapses and they cannot practice until a new application is processed.

**Supply evidence that counts.** Certificates for in-service education should name the topic, date, duration, provider and learning objectives, because the NMBA expects CPD evidence to show the learning need, plan, participation and reflection.
**Do not substitute employer records for the CPD portfolio.** Practitioners must keep their own records, and the NMBA requires evidence of a CPD plan for the previous year if audited.

blocks.text: Employers also use CPD evidence in their own systems. [Credentialing and scope of clinical practice](/regulations/credentialing-and-scope-of-clinical-practice-australia) processes commonly review a practitioner's professional development, and the guide on [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers how to keep that evidence retrievable.

Ahpra and the National Boards audit random samples of practitioners against the mandatory registration standards, including CPD. Ahpra describes a "nationally consistent approach to auditing health practitioners' compliance with mandatory registration standards" on its [audit page](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/Registration/Audit.aspx), which links to board specific audit resources.

For nurses and midwives, the NMBA's [CPD guidelines](https://www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines-Statements/Codes-Guidelines/Guidelines-cpd) require records to be kept "for at least five (5) years from the date you completed the CPD" and available for audit or for an investigation arising from a notification. Evidence must show that the nurse or midwife identified and prioritized learning needs, developed a learning plan, took part in suitable learning activities, and reflected on the value of the learning. Pro rata hours apply when a nurse or midwife registers part-way through the year: at least 5 hours for up to 3 months, rising to 20 hours for 9 to 12 months.

sections.heading: Is a common CPD standard coming?

blocks.text: Possibly, but it has not been approved as at November 2026. Ahpra and 14 National Boards consulted from May 15 to July 17, 2026 on draft revised recency of practice and CPD registration standards. The Medical Board, which requires 50 hours a year, is not participating.

According to Ahpra's [consultation paper](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/documents/default.aspx?record=WD26%2f36029&dbid=AP&chksum=cSwA9u%2bcNJjI79QEoYPEog%3d%3d), the draft common standard would require at least 20 hours of CPD each registration year, including at least 5 hours of interactive CPD with other practitioners, face to face or virtual. Practitioners with scheduled medicines endorsement, endorsed nurses and midwives, and nurse practitioners would complete 10 additional hours, and psychologists 10 additional hours of peer consultation. Practitioners would keep a CPD portfolio of goals, activities and reflections for five years, and CPD on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural safety would be encouraged. The Chiropractic, Optometry, Osteopathy and Podiatry Boards propose removing mandatory first aid and CPR requirements from their standards.

The paper says boards may recommend the revised standards to the Ministerial Council and that, if approved, practitioners "will be provided substantial notice" before they take effect, with transitional arrangements where necessary. Employers should plan for a likely requirement for interactive learning, which favors case discussion, simulation and facilitated sessions over self-paced modules. The guide on [updating training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) sets out how to stage that work.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each board's CPD rule, each employer training obligation and each learning activity as separate, linked elements, so a health service can see which sessions may support CPD for which professions and which only meet an employer duty. When a board standard changes, the affected professions and activities are identified from those links rather than by reviewing every course.

faqs.q: Do practitioners with non-practising registration need to do CPD?
faqs.a: No. Section 128(3) of the National Law excludes practitioners holding non-practising registration from the CPD obligation, and board standards exclude students. Practitioners returning to practice from non-practising registration must instead meet the board's recency of practice requirements and any return to practice conditions.

faqs.q: Can a nurse who is also a midwife count the same activity twice?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is relevant to both. The NMBA requires 20 hours for each profession, 40 in total, but says activities relevant to both nursing and midwifery may be counted as evidence for both. The draft common standard proposed in 2026 keeps the same approach for any practitioner registered in more than one profession.

faqs.q: Does an employer have to check that staff have completed their CPD?
faqs.a: No registration standard imposes that duty on employers. CPD is the practitioner's obligation, declared at renewal and audited by Ahpra. Employers must ensure staff are registered and practising within any conditions, and many review CPD as part of credentialing, performance review or accreditation evidence under their own policies.

faqs.q: What happens if a practitioner does not complete their CPD?
faqs.a: The practitioner must disclose it in the renewal declaration. The Board may then renew without conditions, impose conditions, or refuse renewal under section 112(2)(c) of the National Law. A false declaration is a separate ground for refusal and may lead to conduct action. Boards also grant exemptions in exceptional circumstances.

faqs.q: Do doctors log CPD with Ahpra?
faqs.a: No. Doctors log CPD activities with their AMC accredited CPD home, which can be a specialist college or a non-college provider, and declare which home they used in the previous calendar year when they renew registration. The CPD home oversees completion of the 50 hour requirement.
